Algorithms and theory for PSFs and sparse log-concave factorization

Source: vignettes/articles/algorithm.Rmd
algorithm.Rmd

An ordered multichannel signal can be a mixture of overlapping components. Each component has one profile over the ordered coordinate and one vector of channel loadings. In GC–MS those factors describe how the compound elutes and which ions it produces.

The algorithms below start with sparse deconvolution using a common local response shape. Blind fitting or calibration can estimate that response if needed. The log-concave factorization then allows each retained component to have its own shape, and the simultaneous model can share loadings across samples. Each stage uses the observation likelihood and a criterion for model size.

This article follows the three tutorials: PSF estimation, single-sample factorization and simultaneous multisample factorization. It specifies the actual objectives, coordinate conventions, initialization and acceptance rules.

Common rank-selection objective

For a fitted mean M_s in each sample, logconNMF() searches for nonnegative channel loadings and nonnegative, log-concave profiles that approximately minimize

\begin{aligned} \mathcal J &= -2\sum_s\ell_{\nu_s}(M_s;Y_s)+\kappa\lambda d_{\mathrm{sel}},\\ d_{\mathrm{sel}} &= d_\nu + \begin{cases} mK, & \text{one sample},\\ (m-1)G+L, & \text{simultaneous samples}. \end{cases} \end{aligned}

Here m is the original channel count, K is the single-sample rank, G counts shared spectra and L counts detected sample–component occurrences. A normalized shared spectrum has m-1 free coordinates. Its amplitude in each sample contributes one further coordinate, so G=L=K gives (m-1)K+K=mK. This is a selection penalty on components and occurrences. Profile shapes and smooth backgrounds have no separate charge. The fit can use clustered channels for initialization. The likelihood in the final comparison uses all original channels.

The weighted likelihood and quasi-Poisson score are defined below. The optional working temporal adjustment multiplies the penalty by \kappa, which equals one under independence. The default penalty \lambda=\log(p)\log\log(n) uses the dictionary width and scan count for one sample. For simultaneous fits, both preset inputs equal the total scan count, p=n=\sum_s n_s. A numeric lambda uses the same units in both modes. The reported criteria and simultaneous objective count estimated noise parameters through d_\nu. The single-sample objective omits this additive constant for a fixed noise specification.

Observation model and notation

Let Y=(y_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times m} contain ordered observations, with scans or time points in rows and response channels in columns. Let M=(\mu_{ij}) be the nonnegative mean signal and \nu the shared noise parameters. We use the weighted log likelihood

\ell_\nu(M;Y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m} w_{ij}\ell_\nu(y_{ij};\mu_{ij}),\qquad w_{ij}\geq0.

For quasipoisson, \ell_\nu denotes the scaled Poisson quasi-likelihood kernel defined in the noise-model section. Observation weights are applied once in this definition. The seven supported identity-link models use their own mean-variance relationships and likelihood derivatives; estimation and acceptance take place on the original observation scale.

Throughout, n is the number of original observations, m the original channel count and p the number of candidate PSF columns. B is a nonnegative low-dimensional background basis, A\geq0 its coefficients, and O known additive signal. The notation matches the GCMSprime mathematical basis, which develops the chromatographic interpretation of these models.

Convolution and PSF estimation

Deconvolution based on a known peak shape

Let C\in\mathbb R_+^{p\times m} be a spike-amplitude matrix and g a known point spread function (PSF), or peak shape function. The fixed-kernel mean model is

M=X(g)C+BA+O,\qquad C,A\geq0.

For a constant kernel, X(g)_{ir}=g_{i-r}, with the specified centering and boundary convention. A nonzero row calls a candidate peak using information from every response channel. The grouped L_0 selection target is

\begin{aligned} s(C)&=\|C\|_{2,0} =\sum_{r=1}^{p}\mathbf1\{\|C_{r\cdot}\|_2>0\},\\ \mathcal G(C,A;g) &=-2\ell_\nu\{X(g)C+BA+O;Y\}+\lambda_g s(C). \end{aligned}

Here \lambda_g is the total row-selection charge. This is the target for best subset of groups selection (BSGS), where a group consists of all channel coefficients at one candidate position. Independent selection instead uses \sum_{rj}\mathbf1\{C_{rj}\ne0\}. Background terms are compulsory and unpenalized in the coefficient updates.

L0glm approximates these sparse-selection objectives with adaptive ridge within GLM IRLS, followed by optional relaxed refitting. Its GIC preset supplies the information-criterion scale

\lambda_{\rm IC}=\log p\,\log\log n,

with natural logarithms; AIC uses 2 and BIC uses \log n. The high-dimensional GIC scale follows Fan & Tang (2013). The working adaptive ridge uses a quarter of the selection scale with the appropriate dispersion factor. See L0glm’s algorithm for the inverse-square updates and their quadratic calibration. The grouped candidate fit supplies a support for the factorization; its final rank-selection criterion has an explicit original-channel compound charge.

The sparse pulse-train formulation was inspired by de Rooi & Eilers (2011). Our extensions add the information-criterion regularization preset, grouped selection approximating BSGS, and Poisson or overdispersed Poisson observation models. With estimated quasipoisson dispersion, the corresponding target is quasi-GIC, using the same row-support penalty and a scaled quasi-likelihood.

Relation to convolutive NMF

Cichocki et al. write convolutive NMF (CNMF) as

Y=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}A_\ell Z^{(\ell)}+E,

where Z^{(\ell)} shifts a nonnegative source matrix along its ordered coordinate and A_\ell\geq0 is a lag-specific basis matrix. The constant-PSF model above has the exact transposed representation

\{X(g)C\}^{\mathsf T} =\sum_\ell (g_\ell I_m)(C^{\mathsf T})^{(\ell)}.

It is therefore a constrained CNMF with A_\ell=g_\ell I_m: all channels share one scalar kernel and there is no lag-dependent channel mixing. If the spike-amplitude matrix is further factorized as C=ZP, where P contains component spectra, then

\{X(g)ZP\}^{\mathsf T} =\sum_\ell \underbrace{(g_\ell P^{\mathsf T})}_{A_\ell} (Z^{\mathsf T})^{(\ell)}.

Thus blind constant-PSF estimation is a highly constrained, lag-separable convolutive-NMF problem as well as a sparse multichannel blind-deconvolution problem. This classification does not extend indiscriminately to every stage: calibration from isolated standards estimates a kernel without an NMF; smoothly time-varying PSFs are shift-variant and only locally convolutional; and the final factorization estimates independent component- and sample-specific log-concave profiles rather than shifted copies of one kernel. Here CNMF is reserved for convolutive NMF.

Calibration with isolated peaks

For a local isolated standard peak, write

\mu_{ij}=b_{ij}+o_{ij}+h_i s_j, \qquad h_i>0,\quad s_j\geq0,\quad D^2\log h\leq0.

A low-quantile spline estimates background. Signal-to-noise, separation and profile geometry identify informative peak windows. A native constrained log-profile update fits each window on the original observation scale. Normalize its profile, align by centroid, and resample onto the sample’s median scan interval. A high quantile of fitted profile support widths supplies the common support when control$L is omitted. control$L fixes an odd length.

Algorithm P1 — standard PSF calibration

  1. Resolve the shared noise parameters, weights and additive offsets. Optionally aggregate channels; carry the corresponding sum-model parameters.
  2. Estimate a lower-quantile background and detect informative isolated peaks.
  3. For each retained local window, initialize s_j from positive integrated signal and h from its positive total trace projected to log concavity.
  4. Update \eta=\log h under D^2\eta\leq0, using the likelihood score and positive working curvature. Backtrack against the original likelihood.
  5. Set h\leftarrow h/\sum_i h_i, align its centroid, and place it on the common lag grid. Infer support from fitted peak mass or use the supplied length.
  6. Interpolate the calibrated log kernels at the requested PSF anchor positions, normalize and construct the nonnegative sparse convolution design.

Alternating blind estimation

For a fixed channel spike train c_j, convolution is linear in the kernel:

X(g)c_j=T(c_j)g,

where T(c_j) contains shifted copies of the spike train. This gives a second nonnegative GLM. Blind estimation therefore alternates two L0glm fits: one estimates spike trains and background given the current kernel; the other estimates the kernel given those spike trains. They form an alternating block-coordinate procedure for the joint sparse-likelihood target

\mathcal G(C,A,g) =-2\ell_\nu\{X(g)C+BA+O;Y\}+\lambda_g s(C),

under nonnegativity and a normalized, log-concave kernel. The conditional updates use adaptive ridge and kernel shape smoothing. Their complete spike/background reconstructions are compared using the requested IC.

The PSF fit’s ridge center is the current kernel. The implementation normalizes each informative channel’s spike train for conditioning and rescales the prior center consistently. Positive starts retain kernel tails. Its default kernel update keeps alternating lag positions as compulsory terms; the remaining positions use adaptive selection. A log-concave smoother and centroid alignment produce the kernel proposal, which is normalized to unit sum.

Completed proposals are compared after re-estimating their spike trains and backgrounds. A full-tail proposal and a pedestal-removed proposal can both be considered. The returned checkpoint is the synchronized spike/background fit with the lowest requested criterion among these completed candidates.

Both fits use the same observation model and resolved noise parameters. For fixed-dispersion quasipoisson counts, weighting the Poisson log likelihood by 1/\phi gives the same mean-dependent quasi-likelihood. This allows the native Poisson backend to retain the calibrated noise scale. The other families use their corresponding likelihoods. The kernel updates and completed checkpoint comparisons approximate the joint selection problem.

Algorithm P2 — blind constant-PSF estimation

  1. Set g^{(0)} to the supplied/calibrated kernel, or a normalized Gaussian on the requested lag grid. Resolve shared noise parameters once in estimatePSF().
  2. For t=0,\ldots,T-1:
    1. Construct X(g^{(t)}). Fit [X(g^{(t)}),B] to Y, with compulsory background and the chosen sparse/grouped GLM preset.
    2. Store this spike/background fit and its criterion.
    3. For every informative channel, construct T(c_j) and fit its kernel using background plus known signal as offset, the current kernel as ridge center, and the same observation weights/noise model.
    4. Smooth, recenter and normalize the channel kernels; combine informative channel estimates. Construct the optional concentrated alternative.
    5. Refit spike/background models for the competing proposals and select the better completed candidate.
    6. Stop if \|g^{(t+1)}-g^{(t)}\|_1/\|g^{(t)}\|_1<\epsilon.
  3. Synchronize the last kernel with a spike/background refit. Return the best scored checkpoint, its sparse design and its selection trace.

control$maxiter bounds this loop and control$tol is \epsilon. method="auto" runs P1 followed by P2; "standard" runs P1 and "blind" runs P2. A supplied kernel with maxiter=0L constructs its design directly.

Smoothly time-varying kernels

With nwindows>1L, run local estimation in overlapping windows centered at \tau_1<\cdots<\tau_R. Use a common lag grid and interpolate adjacent log kernels:

\eta_t=(1-a)\log g_r+a\log g_{r+1},\quad a=u^2(3-2u),\quad u=\frac{t-\tau_r}{\tau_{r+1}-\tau_r}, \qquad g_t=\frac{\exp\eta_t}{\sum_\ell\exp\eta_{t\ell}}.

A convex combination of concave log profiles is concave; normalization changes only its intercept. The smoothstep weights give zero interpolation slope at anchor joins. Each design column uses its position’s kernel, is projected to contiguous log-concave support, and is normalized after boundary truncation. The measured observations stay on their scan grid; kernels are indexed in scans.

Algorithm P3 — windowed PSF estimation

  1. Choose evenly spaced sample anchor positions and overlapping local windows.
  2. Run P1/P2 for each anchor, retaining a common lag grid and its diagnostics.
  3. Interpolate log kernels using the weights above, with endpoint continuation.
  4. Place each local kernel at its candidate impulse position, truncate at the observation boundary, enforce log concavity and normalize the column.
  5. Return sparse X, anchor kernels, times, widths and convergence diagnostics.

These PSFs describe a common response at each position. The factorization below subsequently estimates component-specific shapes.

Single-sample model and rank criterion

For scans i, channels j and compounds r,

\mu_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^K H_{ir}S_{rj}+(BA)_{ij}+O_{ij},\qquad H,S,A\geq0.

The columns of H have unit sum, contiguous support and \Delta^2\log H_{\cdot r}\leq0. Spectra S therefore have the interpretation of discrete integrated channel intensities. The objective is

J(H,S,A,K)=-2\ell_\nu(HS+BA+O;Y)+\lambda_RK, \qquad \lambda_R=m\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}.

Here m is the original channel count, \nu contains pooled noise parameters and \kappa=1 for independent observations. The GIC preset uses \lambda_{\rm IC}=\log p\,\log\log n, resolved from the original PSF design and observation count. For numeric lambda equal to c in logconNMF(), the compound charge is \lambda_R=m\kappa c. The single-sample solver splogconNMF() accepts the total compound charge before temporal adjustment.

Dividing by the original channel count gives the equivalent criterion

J/m=-2\ell_\nu/m+\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}K.

Thus each compound contributes one rank-selection unit on the average-channel likelihood scale. Background coefficients and profile complexity receive no additional penalty under this compound-count convention. Channel aggregation retains the original m in \lambda_R; changing the number of outcome groups does not redefine the compound penalty.

Reported information criteria

Let d_\nu count estimated shared noise parameters. The reported IC methods use the selection complexity d_{\rm sel}=mK+d_\nu:

\operatorname{IC}=-2\ell_\nu +\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}(mK+d_\nu).

For a fit using the matching IC preset, this equals J+\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}d_\nu. The extra term is constant when comparing ranks with the same noise specification. Known noise parameters add no selection count. The reported count implements the compound-selection convention; it leaves profile ordinates and smooth background coefficients unpenalized. logLik(), AIC(), BIC(), GIC(), EBIC() and MBIC() use the fitted likelihood and this count. Quasipoisson returns the corresponding quasi-information criteria through the same method names.

Log-concave component-specific profiles

On a regular grid, the shape constraint is H_{ir}^2\geq H_{i-1,r}H_{i+1,r} at interior positive ordinates. On an irregular grid, successive slopes of \log H_{\cdot r} in actual time must be nonincreasing. Each component has contiguous support. This accommodates Gaussian, exponentially modified Gaussian and asymmetric triangular or shark-fin-shaped chromatographic profiles. Gaussian and exponential profiles are log-concave, and convolution preserves this property (Saumard & Wellner, 2014).

Log-concavity implies unimodality and supplies additional control over the rising and falling slopes. It provides stronger shape information than the unimodality constraints commonly used in MCR-ALS (de Juan, Jaumot & Tauler, 2014). Estimating each profile separately allows compound- and concentration-dependent broadening and tailing around the common PSF-based initialization.

Generalized matrix factorization

The broad statistical setting is generalized matrix factorization (GMF): an exponential-family mean is linked to a low-rank product, optionally with observed covariate effects and offsets. See Kidziński et al. (2022) and Castiglione et al. (2026). For example, the latter mean-model structure is

g(\mu)=X_{\rm row}B_{\rm row}^{\top} +B_{\rm col}X_{\rm col}^{\top}+UV^{\top}+O.

Our model uses the identity link, U=H, V^{\top}=S, and X_{\rm row}=B, B_{\rm row}^{\top}=A for the smooth background; the column-covariate term is omitted. It adds nonnegativity, unit-area log-concave profiles and a compound-count penalty to select the rank. This gives a sparse log-concave nonnegative GMF with automatic rank selection.

Deviance matrix factorization and Bregman NMF

logconNMF() fits a rank-penalized, nonnegative deviance matrix factorization with log-concave profiles. It belongs to the deviance-based framework of Wang & Carvalho (2023), using an identity link for the additive mean \mu=HS+BA+O. The loss also connects directly to NMF with Bregman divergences.

For a regular exponential-dispersion model with fixed noise parameters,

\ell(y;\vartheta,\phi)=\frac{y\vartheta-b(\vartheta)}{\phi}+c(y,\phi), \qquad \mu=b'(\vartheta),

let \Psi=b^* be the convex conjugate of b. Its Bregman divergence is

D_\Psi(y,\mu)=\Psi(y)-\Psi(\mu)-\Psi'(\mu)(y-\mu).

Since \Psi'(\mu)=\vartheta(\mu) and \Psi(\mu)=\mu\vartheta(\mu)-b\{\vartheta(\mu)\}, substitution gives

\begin{aligned} D_\Psi(y,\mu) &=y\vartheta(y)-b\{\vartheta(y)\}-y\vartheta(\mu)+b\{\vartheta(\mu)\},\\ 2\{\ell(y;y,\phi)-\ell(y;\mu,\phi)\} &=\frac{2}{\phi}D_\Psi(y,\mu). \end{aligned}

Here the likelihood on the second line is written in mean coordinates. Boundary observations use the corresponding limits. Thus, conditional on the noise parameters, fitting is equivalent to minimizing

2\sum_{ij}\frac{w_{ij}}{\phi}D_\Psi(y_{ij},(HS+BA+O)_{ij}) +\lambda_RK

under the nonnegativity, profile-normalization and log-concavity constraints. The saturated likelihood contributes a constant in these conditional model comparisons. The corresponding divergences include:

Noise model Generator \Psi(u) Half unit deviance D_\Psi(y,\mu)
Gaussian u^2/2 (y-\mu)^2/2
Poisson u\log u-u y\log(y/\mu)-y+\mu
Gamma, uncensored y>0 -\log u y/\mu-\log(y/\mu)-1
NB2, fixed shape \theta u\log u-(u+\theta)\log(u+\theta) y\log(y/\mu)-(y+\theta)\log\{(y+\theta)/(\mu+\theta)\}

For NB2, \phi=1 and the shape \theta enters the generator. Gaussian, Poisson and Gamma therefore give squared-error, generalized KL and Itakura–Saito NMF losses. Quasipoisson gives the KL kernel scaled by its dispersion. Censored Gamma and the mean-dependent-shape extensions use their full likelihood kernels described below; estimated noise parameters are compared using the full likelihood as well.

Smooth background and flexible noise models

The additive background BA uses a nonnegative, low-dimensional B-spline basis, or a constant basis for a short window. Its coefficients are compulsory and unpenalized. Conditional background updates retain the fitted component signal in the offset and use the specified observation likelihood. For chromatograms the basis should vary much more slowly than an individual peak. A lower-quantile background fit initializes isolated-peak calibration.

Seven identity-link signal models

Noise model Variance Negative log-likelihood score in the mean
Gaussian \phi (\mu-y)/\phi
Poisson \mu 1-y/\mu
Quasipoisson \phi\mu (1-y/\mu)/\phi
NB2 \mu+\mu^2/\theta \theta(\mu-y)/\{\mu(\mu+\theta)\}
Gamma \phi\mu^2 (\mu-y)/(\phi\mu^2)
NB1 \phi\mu \{\psi(a)-\psi(a+y)+\log\phi\}/(\phi-1), a=\mu/(\phi-1)
Common-scale Gamma b_0\mu \{\psi(\mu/b_0)+\log b_0-\log y\}/b_0

The final two models use the exact distributions documented in signal_families. Their observed positive curvatures are differences of trigamma functions for NB1 and \psi_1(\mu/b_0)/b_0^2 for common-scale Gamma. The latter is convex in the mean; the NB1 curvature is nonnegative because trigamma decreases on the positive real line. At \phi=1, NB1 uses its Poisson limit. The Gamma scores in the table apply to positive, uncensored observations; zero observations use the censoring likelihood below. Gaussian variance is \sigma^2=\phi; common-scale Gamma uses b_0 for its shared scale.

Poisson, NB1 and NB2 require integer counts. Quasipoisson accepts nonnegative continuous intensities; Gaussian observations may also be negative, while the modeled component signal remains nonnegative. Gamma observations below the detection threshold are represented by zero.

logconNMF() defaults to poisson("identity") for count-data factorization. estimatePSF() defaults to quasipoisson("identity"). For GC/MS electron-multiplier intensities, GCMSprime uses the latter as its workflow default and reuses the estimated noise specification during PSF estimation and factorization.

Quasipoisson and estimated overdispersion

Poisson ion arrivals combined with random electron-multiplier gain motivate an overdispersed counting model. For independent identically distributed gains G_a, independent of N,

Y=\sum_{a=1}^{N}G_a,\quad N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\Lambda),\qquad \operatorname{E}(Y)=\Lambda\operatorname{E}(G),\quad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\Lambda\operatorname{E}(G^2).

The variance-to-mean ratio depends on gain and intensity units. A quasipoisson working model retains this proportional variance structure; electronics and digitization can add further variation. See Ipsen (2015) for the physical measurement model.

With a resolved common dispersion \widehat\phi, the implemented scaled kernel is

\ell_Q(M;Y)=\frac{1}{\widehat\phi}\sum_{ij}w_{ij} \{y_{ij}\log\mu_{ij}-\mu_{ij}-\log\Gamma(y_{ij}+1)\}.

The final term is constant for fixed observations and scale. It therefore gives the same model comparisons as the mean-dependent quasi-likelihood in GCMSprime. Equivalently, write

\begin{aligned} D_P(Y,M)&=2\sum_{ij}w_{ij} \{y_{ij}\log(y_{ij}/\mu_{ij})-y_{ij}+\mu_{ij}\},\\ J_Q&=D_P(Y,M)/\widehat\phi+\lambda_RK+\text{constant}. \end{aligned}

Use 0\log(0/\mu)=0. Thus the same original-channel rank charge applies to GIC and quasi-GIC; the estimated dispersion scales the fit term. logLik() marks the quasipoisson kernel with quasi=TRUE, and the regular IC method names return quasi-information criteria.

Pooled noise calibration

Noise parameters are shared across channels. With dispersion=NULL, the marginal variance or scale is estimated from fourth- and eighth-order temporal differences in quieter regions of a smoothed pilot signal. Supplying a positive dispersion fixes it. NB2 similarly supports a fixed positive theta, automatic pooled initialization with theta=NULL, or a negative starting value that enables subsequent likelihood-improving shape updates. Poisson and NB2 have GLM scale dispersion one; NB2 overdispersion is represented by \theta.

Candidate rank or grouping moves are compared using the same resolved noise parameters, observation weights, offsets and numerical penalty. An enabled NB2 shape update is a separate likelihood-improving step; the next candidate comparison uses that updated common shape. This keeps each acceptance test on a common noise scale. The temporal-variation section details the marginal variance and optional correlation adjustment.

Censored Gamma intensities

Recorded zeros may represent intensities below a detection limit d, whose contribution is \log P(Y<d;\mu). Positive observations contribute their ordinary density. For standard Gamma, set a=1/\phi, z=d/(\phi\mu); its negative log-CDF derivative is

g(\mu)=\frac{z^a e^{-z}}{\Gamma(a)P(a,z)\mu}.

For common-scale Gamma, z=d/b_0 stays fixed and a=\mu/b_0 changes. The convergent incomplete-Gamma series

P(a,z)=\frac{e^{-z}z^a}{\Gamma(a+1)} \left\{1+\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{z^k}{(a+1)\cdots(a+k)}\right\}

provides its shape derivative when z is small. The general branch uses the Gamma CDF and a numerical shape derivative. Both branches are checked against the actual censored likelihood. The default detection limit is 0.5 intensity units and can be changed through control$censor.

Local quadratic updates

For a coefficient b\geq0, keep the rest of the signal in an offset r_i and write \mu_i=r_i+x_i b. With negative log-likelihood score g_i and positive working curvature I_i, propose

b^+=\max\left\{0,b-\frac{\sum_i w_i x_i g_i} {\sum_i w_i x_i^2 I_i}\right\}.

Actual-loss backtracking and a zero-boundary check complete each scalar solve. The Poisson branch uses a faster bracketed likelihood solve. Its score \sum_iw_ix_i(1-y_i/\mu_i) is monotone, and its nonnegative root is bounded above by \sum_iw_iy_i/\sum_iw_ix_i. Channels are independent conditional on the profiles, allowing deterministic OpenMP parallelism.

Local profile updates use the original observation likelihood. For \eta_i=\log h_i, \mu_{ij}=r_{ij}+h_i s_j, the chain-rule score and working information are

g_{\eta,i}=h_i\sum_jw_{ij}s_jg_{\mu,ij},\qquad I_{\eta,i}=h_i^2\sum_jw_{ij}s_j^2I_{\mu,ij}.

The working target is \eta_i-g_{\eta,i}/I_{\eta,i}, with tiny stabilization where the information vanishes. This quadratic approximation updates the log profile parameters; the observed intensities remain on their original scale and acceptance uses their actual likelihood.

A smooth concave log profile can be written as

\eta(t)=a+bt-\frac12\sum_j c_j \{(t-u_j)_+^2-(t-v_j)_+^2\},\qquad c_j\geq0,

where the intervals [u_j,v_j) partition the local time window. Its second derivative is -\sum_jc_j\mathbf1_{[u_j,v_j)}(t)\leq0, giving hard log-concavity. The intercept and slope are unrestricted, and a small nonnegative quadratic solve estimates the curvature coefficients. For more detailed local adjustments, piecewise-linear log-profile increments preserve the existing fine-scale curvature; a concave-envelope projection removes numerical constraint residuals. Backtracking between feasible log profiles preserves concavity and accepts only likelihood improvements.

The scaled active-set quadratic solver uses Cholesky factorizations for positive-definite active subproblems. Extended-precision residuals provide iterative corrections through the same factor. Conditioning and residual checks trigger a rank-revealing QR fallback when needed. The quadratic objective and shape constraints define the numerical subproblem.

For a piecewise-linear log profile, each row of the interpolation matrix has at most two nonzero entries. Its weighted Gram matrix is tridiagonal, so natural-order sparse Cholesky and sparse slope-constraint products avoid dense arithmetic on structural zeros. Successive scoring steps initialize the inequality solver at its preceding feasible solution and use a common KKT tolerance.

For a fixed component spectrum, a zero loading makes that channel’s contribution constant in the profile update. Native workspaces therefore retain its positive-loading channels in their original order. Spectral updates and complete model comparisons still use every original channel.

Small joint conditional Poisson spectral and background refits use observed-curvature Newton steps. Successive steps continue the constrained active set, reuse fixed gradient scales and exploit sparse weighted products for localized profiles. Conditional likelihood backtracking verifies each step, with boundary checks and a KKT tolerance controlling convergence.

The spectra act as covariates in each local profile update: Y_{\mathcal W}^{T}=S_{\mathcal B}^{T}H_{\mathcal W,\mathcal B}^{T} +R_{\mathcal W}^{T}. The current profiles and spectra provide the starts. Fine refinement uses the constrained log-profile quadratic directly, with no extra shrinkage toward zero or toward the initial PSF. Profile normalization transfers its scale into the corresponding spectrum. Every local block covers the full support of every component whose spectrum is updated.

Fusion starts with spectral compatibility and profile overlap. Broad-anchor and contained-tail proposals are refined only within the affected windows; other compounds remain in an offset. The full original-channel criterion decides whether each proposed rank change is retained. A final conservative pass can reunite broad profiles with complementary ion sets when their profile cosine is at least 0.95. Neighbouring modes are guarded during its local refit. control=list(profile_cycles=0L) disables the main shape-refinement stage; control=list(profile_fusion=FALSE) disables the final conservative pass.

A contained fragment can have a different profile from its broad parent while carrying almost the same spectrum. The final contained-fragment search therefore uses spectral cosine at least 0.97, at least 99% of the fragment’s profile mass within the parent’s 1%-height interval, and a fragment area no larger than 15% of the parent’s area. The parent FWHM must exceed four times the representative PSF FWHM. A parent-profile start and a log-concave combined-profile start are both tried. Each candidate and an unmerged control receive six local joint-refinement cycles, with four profile scoring steps per cycle. The complete original-channel criterion chooses between them. This prevents refinement gains alone from being attributed to a reduction in rank.

Complete the fit on the original ion channels

The final pass checks conditional deletions, fusions of overlapping profiles, and PSF candidates suggested by the original-channel residuals. Nearly proportional profiles can be considered even when neither is a broad peak. Candidate construction uses matrix products and performs no refitting. Accepted proposals use native local likelihood fits with all other compounds and the fitted background held in the offset.

For J=-2\ell_\nu+\lambda_RK, let \Delta D=-2\{\ell_\nu(M';Y)-\ell_\nu(M;Y)\}. A deletion has change \Delta J=\Delta D-\lambda_R, a fusion of r factors has \Delta J=\Delta D-\lambda_R(r-1), and an addition has \Delta J=\Delta D+\lambda_R. The complete original-channel criterion must improve. Noise parameters, offsets, weights and the numerical compound penalty stay fixed. Cached deletion scores need updating only for profiles whose temporal supports overlap the deleted factor.

The pass uses bounded scan windows to screen missed peaks, then refines the accepted profiles locally under hard log concavity. The same procedure is available for every supported noise family; working-score screening proposes candidates and each family’s likelihood decides acceptance. The returned fit$cleanup records the moves and full objective change. control=list(original_cleanup=FALSE) skips this pass.

Fusion, aggregation and rank selection

The estimated PSF supplies candidate shapes. Grouped sparse deconvolution, fusion of spectrally similar overlapping components under log-concavity, and local likelihood refinement jointly select a parsimonious factorization rank. This yields a data-driven estimate of the underlying number of components. Its distinctive feature is the integration of these operations with an explicit noise-aware compound-count objective.

  1. Obtain a variance-matched grouped deconvolution start, retaining the spline background as compulsory unpenalized terms.
  2. Compare normalized spectra by Jensen–Shannon information loss. Propose fusions when their elution profiles overlap and their combined profile can be made log-concave. Clustering itself performs no regression fits.
  3. Refine each proposal locally, holding all outside contributions fixed. Overlapping spectra and the candidate profile can adjust together.
  4. Accept a rank change when -2\{\ell_\nu(M';Y)-\ell_\nu(M;Y)\}+\lambda_R(K'-K)\leq0.
  5. Update broad profiles, smooth background coefficients and spectra, followed by final boundary checks and rank pruning.

Algebraic fusion uses a least concave majorant of the log profile, followed by normalization. Local likelihood updates impose hard concavity constraints in their quadratic solves. Every complete accepted stage decreases the actual criterion, within numerical tolerance. history and ledger_error make this property directly checkable.

With precluster=32L, the initial workflow uses at most 32 aggregated outcome groups. Size factors colSums(pmax(Y,0)) account for different total ion intensities. \lambda_R retains the original channel count, and final refinement and rank checks return to every original channel. Poisson sums remain Poisson; common-dispersion quasipoisson sums retain their mean-variance relationship. Independent Gaussian variances add. Independent NB1 variables sharing \pi=1/\phi, with \phi>1, are closed under sums, because their probability-generating functions multiply as

\prod_j\left\{\frac{\pi}{1-(1-\pi)t}\right\}^{\mu_j/(\phi-1)} =\left\{\frac{\pi}{1-(1-\pi)t}\right\}^{\sum_j\mu_j/(\phi-1)}.

The same property holds for common-scale Gamma latent signals, through \prod_j(1+b_0t)^{-\mu_j/b_0}=(1+b_0t)^{-\sum_j\mu_j/b_0}. Standard NB2 and Gamma use moment matching in the reduced problem. For channel intensity fractions r_j within a group G,

\theta_G=\theta/\sum_{j\in G}r_j^2,\qquad \phi_G=\phi\sum_{j\in G}r_j^2,

respectively. These match the aggregate variance under the working channel proportions. Censoring or different channel weights also give working aggregate approximations; final scoring uses the original responses and their specified model.

Temporal variation

High-order differences suppress the slowly varying mean. With a_k=(-1)^k{r\choose k} and stationary covariance c_h,

\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\Delta^r e)}{{2r\choose r}} =c_0+2\sum_{h=1}^r(-1)^h \frac{{2r\choose r+h}}{{2r\choose r}}c_h.

The identity follows by expanding the variance and using \sum_k a_k a_{k+h}=(-1)^h{2r\choose r+h}. With lag-one covariance this reduces to c_0-2r c_1/(r+1). Fourth and eighth differences estimate the marginal variance and lag-one covariance. The optional penalty multiplier \kappa=1+2\widehat\rho_1 approximates the local information loss for smooth directions, while the marginal scale stays in the component likelihood. This is a scalar working covariance adjustment. Composite-likelihood theory relates the broader correction to \operatorname{tr}(JH^{-1}), where H is sensitivity and J is score covariance (Varin, Reid & Firth, 2011).

Single-sample algorithm

Let \mathcal L=-\ell_\nu(M;Y). Resolve the pooled noise parameters \nu and information multiplier \kappa before rank comparisons. The default initializer uses a positive smoothed mean \widetilde\mu and variance-matched Poisson working weights

w^{\rm pilot}_{ij}=w_{ij}\, \frac{\widetilde\mu_{ij}}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid\widetilde\mu_{ij},\nu)}.

It fits grouped nonnegative l0glmFit() on the PSF design with compulsory background, using the unadjusted \lambda_{\rm IC}. The starting search and original-channel polish use J_0=-2\ell_\nu+m\lambda_{\rm IC}K. This permissive initialization preserves candidates while the profiles are refined. Final rank comparisons use J=-2\ell_\nu+m\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}K. When \kappa=1, the two criteria coincide. A supplied start with profiles, spectra and optional background coefficients bypasses screening. The working Poisson fit initializes the factorization; complete rank decisions use J with the specified observation model.

Algorithm N1 — sparse log-concave NMF with rank selection

  1. Normalize candidate PSF columns. Resolve the noise scale, optional lag-one information adjustment, weights, offsets and background basis.
  2. If preclustering is requested:
    1. Form size-adjusted outcome groups and sum their observations/offsets.
    2. Construct the corresponding exact or moment-matched aggregate noise model.
    3. Initialize and fuse components in that reduced space, retaining the original channel count in m\lambda_{\rm IC}.
    4. Lift loadings/background with group intensity fractions; return to every original channel for likelihood refinement.
  3. Otherwise obtain the variance-matched grouped deconvolution start directly. Normalize each profile and transfer its scale into its loadings.
  4. Run the bounded local refinement stages:
    1. Hold other components and background fixed in a local offset. Update each spectrum by nonnegative scalar likelihood solves, including zero-boundary checks; update each concave log profile with the quadratic subroutine below.
    2. Update nonnegative background coefficients conditionally on the component signal. Preserve the specified family likelihood.
    3. Generate spectral/overlap-compatible fusion candidates algebraically, starting with stronger components. Refine only the affected scan windows.
    4. Accept whole initialization candidates only if their complete J_0 decreases within numerical tolerance. Check conditional deletions and zero spectra.
    5. If NB2 shape updating is enabled, propose bounded steps in \log\theta and backtrack until the original likelihood improves.
  5. On all original channels, run fine constrained profile/spectrum updates, conditional deletions, compatible fusions and residual-supported additions. Polish the accepted profiles again and revisit retained narrow-fragment candidates under J_0.
  6. Restore the requested information multiplier and evaluate the resulting initialization under J. Test contained fragments of broad components against equally refined unmerged local controls. Accept only complete original-channel improvements under this fixed final criterion.
  7. For nearly coincident modes, screen left-, right- and two-sided width restarts. Refine promising starts and an unperturbed control on the original channels, retaining a restart only when its complete J improves on both the current fit and the refined control.
  8. Return temporally ordered H,S, background, family/noise parameters, likelihood, rank criterion, stage acceptance ledger and timings.

profile_cycles, fusion_passes and the other stage controls bound the work; local solvers also stop when their score/step change is sufficiently small. The final restart pass is enabled by default when profile_cycles>0 and can be disabled with control=list(profile_restarts=FALSE).

For a profile h with mode a, define T_{l,r}(i)=a+\frac{i-a}{l\,\mathbf1\{i<a\}+r\,\mathbf1\{i\geq a\}}, \qquad h_i'=\frac{\exp\{\eta(T_{l,r}(i))\}} {\sum_t\exp\{\eta(T_{l,r}(t))\}},\quad\eta=\log h. The three starts use (l,r)=(2,1),(1,2),(2,2), with piecewise-linear interpolation of \eta. Concave slopes remain nonincreasing on each side, and their change from nonnegative to nonpositive at the mode preserves log concavity across the join. Candidate pairs have mode separation at most one quarter of both FWHMs. Preliminary screening, refinement and acceptance use the original channels and fixed noise, weights, offsets, background and component count. Thus \Delta J=-2\Delta\ell_\nu for an accepted restart. The profile_starts audit records the input component index, chosen start, score changes and time.

The initialization ledger records its unadjusted criterion. When the final information multiplier differs from one, the final ledger begins at the completed initialization and uses the fixed adjusted criterion throughout. The noise scale remains on its marginal variance scale. The reduced-space search supplies an initializer; final rank checks use every original channel.

Subroutine Q — local likelihood and shape update

  1. Subtract the focus component from the current mean to obtain the fixed offset.
  2. Compute mean-scale likelihood scores and positive working information.
  3. For a loading b, propose a nonnegative scalar scoring step or use the bracketed Poisson root. For a profile, set \eta=\log h, apply the chain-rule scores and solve a weighted quadratic under nonincreasing slopes.
  4. Halve the step until the original likelihood improves and constraints hold. A convex combination of feasible log profiles remains concave.
  5. Normalize the profile, transfer its scale to loadings, and update only the affected mean block. Outside-window observations are unchanged.

For a rank change \Delta K, acceptance is based on

\Delta J=2(\mathcal L_{\rm new}-\mathcal L_{\rm old})+\lambda_R\Delta K.

Because outside-window means are unchanged, their likelihood contributions cancel exactly. Local computation therefore gives the complete objective difference without rescoring unaffected observations.

Simultaneous model on original scan grids

After suppressing backgrounds, exposures and offsets, the multisample mean can be written M_s=Q_sP, where P is shared exactly and Q_s is sample-specific. This is simultaneous NMF in the terminology of Cichocki et al., Badea (2008) and Lee et al. (2012).

For sample s, let u=w_s(t) be its monotone alignment map. Native bin edges t_{si-1/2},t_{si+1/2} define

\Delta u_{si}=w_s(t_{si+1/2})-w_s(t_{si-1/2}),\qquad J_{si}=\frac{\Delta u_{si}}{\Delta t_{si}}.

With known exposure e_{si}>0, the mean model is

\mu_{sij}=e_{si}\left\{J_{si}\sum_g a_{sg}h_{sg}(u_{si})p_{gj} +(B_sA_s)_{ij}\right\}+o_{sij}.

Spectra have p_{gj}\geq0 and \sum_jp_{gj}=1. Each detected profile satisfies

h_{sg}\geq0,\quad \sum_i\Delta u_{si}h_{sg}(u_{si})=1,\quad \frac{\log h_{sg,i+1}-\log h_{sg,i}}{u_{s,i+1}-u_{si}} \text{ is nonincreasing}.

The Jacobian preserves integrated area under alignment. No interpolation or resampling is applied to observations. Local likelihood evaluations use their original channels, weights, offsets and sample-specific noise parameters.

The rank-selection objective is

\mathcal J=-2\sum_s\ell_{\nu_s}(M_s;Y_s) +\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}\{(m-1)G+L+d_\nu\}.

Here G is the number of common spectra and L the number of detected sample-compound occurrences. A unit-sum spectrum contributes m-1 free spectral coordinates and each occurrence contributes an amplitude. d_\nu=\sum_s d_{\nu_s} counts estimated sample-specific noise parameters, each shared across that sample’s channels. Profile and baseline complexity are unpenalized shape-constrained nuisance terms in this rank criterion. The weighted likelihood of each sample follows the observation-model definition above, so observation weights are included once.

For temporal-correlation adjustment, \kappa is the largest resolved sample information factor. Quasipoisson uses each sample’s frozen, scaled Poisson kernel. The same logLik(), AIC(), BIC(), GIC(), EBIC() and MBIC() interfaces apply.

For one sample, G=L=K, so

(m-1)G+L+d_\nu=mK+d_\nu.

At a common preset value and information factor, the simultaneous score therefore reduces to the single-sample reported IC. Both select compound count without an extra penalty on profile complexity or background dimension.

Penalty scale for single and simultaneous fits

Interface IC-name lambda Numeric lambda=c
logconNMF() on one matrix m\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC} per compound m\kappa c per compound
logconNMF() on a sample list \kappa\lambda_{\rm IC} per selection degree of freedom \kappa c per selection degree of freedom

The simultaneous selection count is (m-1)G+L+d_\nu. A compound observed in one sample contributes m-1 spectral coordinates and one amplitude, so its charge matches that of a single-sample component. The single-sample solver splogconNMF() accepts a numeric total compound charge c; enter c/m in logconNMF() to reproduce that charge. Estimated noise parameters add a constant selection count when their specification is fixed. Single-sample presets use their original n,p; simultaneous presets use n_*=p_*=\sum_s n_s.

Alignment and local updates

  1. Fit samples independently, optionally initializing in 32 aggregated channel groups and returning to every original channel.
  2. Match high-confidence spectra to a reference sample. Use the 1%-height peak start plus half the narrow-peak width as the timing anchor.
  3. Fit a robust low-dimensional drift spline, with log area ratio as a nuisance term for concentration-related anchor motion. Retain its drift component and enforce positive slope.
  4. Group spectra algebraically when their timing and area-ordered profile overlap are compatible. Each group has at most one occurrence per sample. This clustering stage performs no NMF or GLM refits.
  5. Update local concave log profiles, pool spectral scores over samples, and update each smooth background. Backtrack against the original likelihood.
  6. Retain a grouped fit when its complete penalized objective improves. Return temporally ordered consensus spectra and sample-specific areas.

For a common spectral coefficient p_{gj}, with design value x_{sgi}=e_{si}J_{si}a_{sg}h_{sg}(u_{si}), the pooled negative-log-likelihood score and positive working information are

U_{gj}=\sum_{si:g\in s}w_{sij}x_{sgi}g_{\mu,sij},\qquad I_{gj}=\sum_{si:g\in s}w_{sij}x_{sgi}^{2}I_{\mu,sij}.

A nonnegative scoring step is followed by full-likelihood backtracking. Renormalizing a spectrum transfers its scale into the occurrence amplitudes and preserves the fitted signal. Profile updates use the corresponding chain-rule score in log coordinates and linear slope constraints on actual aligned times. Native OpenMP updates give identical results across thread counts in the validation examples.

The native spectral kernel evaluates each cell’s likelihood derivatives once and pools them over the sparse profiles in one pass parallelized across channels. Cached peak geometry avoids rescanning every profile after each algebraic merge. Shared row-wise weights and offsets retain one vector throughout the simultaneous fit, with channel-specific matrices used when required.

All seven signal families are supported: Gaussian, Poisson, quasipoisson, NB2, NB1, censored Gamma and common-scale Gamma. Dispersion parameters are resolved from the original channels and frozen for group comparisons. NB2 additionally supports likelihood-improving shape updates when initialized with a negative theta.

Simultaneous algorithm and normalization

For simultaneous models use n_*=p_*=\sum_s n_s in the IC preset, and the largest sample information multiplier as \kappa. Noise parameters are shared across channels within each sample. The joint rank count is (m-1)G+L+d_\nu, reducing to mK+d_\nu when one sample has G=L=K. Common unit-sum spectra contribute m-1 coordinates each; each observed sample-compound occurrence contributes one amplitude.

If \sum_i\Delta u_{si}h_{sg}(u_{si})=1, then

\sum_i\Delta t_{si}J_{si}h_{sg}(u_{si}) =\sum_i\Delta u_{si}h_{sg}(u_{si})=1.

Thus an occurrence amplitude represents integrated intensity in the chosen time unit, before its known exposure is applied. sampleNMF() also returns unit-sum original-grid profiles and their compatible discrete loadings.

Algorithm N2 — simultaneous multisample log-concave NMF

  1. Fit samples independently by N1, or read supplied fitted factors. Persist observations and factor checkpoints sample by sample.
  2. Match high-confidence spectra to a reference. Obtain onset-plus-half-width anchors and fit a robust monotone drift map, accounting for log area ratio as a nuisance predictor of anchor motion. Retain the drift component.
  3. Map each original bin’s edges to aligned time. Compute \Delta u,J, initialize log-concave profiles there, normalize by \Delta u, and put their scale into occurrence amplitudes. Initialize each occurrence with its own spectrum.
  4. Perform initial_cycles of local profile, pooled spectrum and background updates; retain this ungrouped-spectrum reference checkpoint.
  5. For up to rounds grouping rounds:
    1. Restrict spectrum comparisons to nearby aligned time bins. Compare cosine or Hellinger distance, with at most one occurrence per sample per group.
    2. Check area-ordered log-concave-ridge compatibility. Pool compatible spectra by occurrence area. Keep profiles fixed during this algebraic grouping.
    3. Run up to cycles joint local-update cycles: constrained sample profiles; batched, pooled spectral scores; nonnegative sample backgrounds; optional NB2 shape updates. Backtrack each update on original-channel likelihood.
    4. Stop grouping when a subsequent round makes no new joins.
  6. Compare the complete grouped/refined candidate against the reference checkpoint using the joint criterion. Retain the lower-criterion model.
  7. Compact consensus IDs in temporal order. Return shared spectra, sample factors, alignment, diagnostics and an area table with missing occurrences NA.

Clustering constructs a complete candidate before joint refinement. The final comparison includes every original channel and all detected occurrences.

Area-ordered ridge compatibility

Put matched profiles on a small comparison grid for geometry only; observed signals remain on their native grids. Order profiles by total area and allow bounded local alignment. Their thresholded level sets must overlap and support a common log-concave ridge across the area ordering. This screens concentration- dependent broadening and tailing before sharing a spectrum. The subsequent original-data likelihood decides whether the combined proposal is retained.

Streaming and parallel computation

Sparse profile supports restrict work to affected scan windows. The simultaneous spectral kernel evaluates each observation’s likelihood derivatives once and pools them across its active profiles. Channels can be processed independently in OpenMP; sample contributions are accumulated in a fixed order. The main optimization reads one sample at a time, with shared spectra and compact geometry summaries in memory. Shared row weights/offsets retain one vector. RT bins avoid an all-occurrence pairwise similarity matrix.

Methodological foundations and implementation

Sparse pulse-train regression builds on de Rooi & Eilers, and the adaptive ridge initialization uses L0glm’s extensions of reweighted quadratic selection. Eilers’ work motivates positive shape-constrained profiles; generalized and deviance matrix factorization provide the likelihood framework. Bregman and size-adjusted Poisson clustering supply useful spectral and channel geometries.

The likelihood-based hard shape solves, complete original-channel rank moves, windowed kernel checkpoints and simultaneous normalization/acceptance rules above describe the logconNMF algorithms. The simultaneous criterion counts shared spectra and sample-specific amplitudes explicitly. The general references establish the underlying frameworks; the objectives and pseudocode here specify their adaptation to these constrained signal models.

The likelihood distributions follow the R negative-binomial and Gamma parameterizations. The compound-count criterion, local log-concave fusion and their integration with L0glm’s grouped initialization are developments of this package.

Parallel samples and bounded-memory updates

With common spectra P fixed, sample-specific factors are conditionally independent. The simultaneous criterion is

J=-2\sum_s\ell_s(Y_s;\mu_s) +\lambda\{(m-1)G+L+d_{\mathrm{noise}}\},

where G is the number of shared compounds and L the number of detected sample-compound occurrences. Profile and background updates leave this rank charge fixed. They can therefore run concurrently over samples, with each accepted update decreasing its own contribution to the full criterion. Pooled spectral gradients and information are computed per sample and summed in acquisition order. The shared spectral step is accepted against the full original-channel likelihood.

A common channel map has a one-hot membership matrix A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times q}, giving aggregated observations \bar Y_s=Y_sA and spectra \bar P=PA. The map is learned once from summed time-bin counts or supplied as a saved channelGroups() object. Only this map-learning step uses a common time grid. The fitting grids, bin exposures and sparse PSF matrices X_s remain sample specific.

For Poisson and common-scale quasipoisson observations with shared scan weights, channel sums provide inexpensive profile proposals. Each proposal is checked on all original channels in its affected time window. Other families retain their original-channel profile objective. Spectral, background and likelihood passes read at most 32 original channels per block through a native binary-matrix reader. Thus aggregation accelerates the proposal and matching steps while the target criterion continues to use the original observations.

The execution order is:

  1. Learn or load the common channel map.
  2. Fit independent samples concurrently, each with its own sparse PSF.
  3. Estimate alignment and build the common spectral candidate graph.
  4. With spectra fixed, update profiles and backgrounds independently across samples; calculate pooled spectral contributions concurrently.
  5. Reduce contributions in sample order and update the shared spectra.
  6. Group compatible occurrences, refreshing only graph edges incident to a merged root. Distances and ordering of unaffected proposals are retained.
  7. Accept the complete candidate using the original-channel penalized objective and return full spectra, original-grid profiles and integrated areas.

ncores is a total logical-CPU budget. With W concurrent sample workers, each receives \lfloor\texttt{ncores}/W\rfloor native threads. BLAS runs with one thread during batch fitting and its caller setting is restored afterwards. Only the assigned sample and compact factors are sent to each worker; the complete observation cache is never serialized to every worker.

The resident observation cache uses 8q\sum_s n_s bytes. For 1,000 samples with 10,000 scans and 32 groups, this is 2.56 GB, plus factors and active-worker buffers. Original observations and factor checkpoints are disk backed. Sparse sample-specific PSFs are modest in size: a measured 14,946-by-14,946 design with 1.47 million stored nonzero values occupied 16.9 MiB.
